title: Statistical Hypothesis Tests: Mean, Proportion & Goodness of Fit
sub: Lecture 10 · Seminar 11 · H0 and H1, five steps, t- and z-tests, chi-square goodness-of-fit
blurb: Null and alternative hypotheses, significance level, the five steps of every test, rejection regions, t- and z-tests of the mean, the z-test of a proportion and the chi-square goodness-of-fit test.
h1: Statistical Hypothesis Tests: Mean, Proportion & Goodness of Fit
lede: A hypothesis test uses one random sample to judge a claim about a whole population. Every test in 4ST601 follows the same five steps; what changes is the test statistic and which tail of the distribution the rejection region is in.
six: **H0** says the parameter equals a value; **H1** says >, < or ≠.
Five steps: H0/H1 → test statistic → its value → **rejection region** → **conclusion** in words.
Value in W: “**inconsistent with H0 in favour of H1**”; otherwise “**not inconsistent with H0**”.
**H1 decides the tail**: > right, < left, ≠ both tails with α/2.
Normal population, σ² unknown → **t(n − 1)**; large sample or proportion → **z**.
**Goodness of fit**: g = Σ (n − n′)²/n′, n′ = nπ0, df = k − 1, always the right tail.
must: The five steps, choosing the tail, and the t-, z- and goodness-of-fit tests
foot: Source: 4ST601 Seminar 11 exercise file (worked procedure and conclusions) and the official formula sheet, page 7. TODO: verify against the Lecture 10 slides when they are added.

questions.q: What does the null hypothesis H0 state in a test of a population mean?
questions.answer: The mean equals the claimed value, e.g. E(X) = 3,500 g
wrong: The mean is lower than the claimed value
The mean differs from the claimed value
questions.e: H0 always contains the equality; the alternative H1 contains >, < or ≠.

questions.q: What is the significance level α?
questions.answer: The accepted probability of wrongly rejecting a true H0
wrong: The probability that H0 is true
The width of the confidence interval
questions.e: α is the risk you accept of rejecting H0 although it is true (type 1 error).

questions.q: Which is the correct order of the steps of a hypothesis test?
questions.answer: H0 and H1 → test statistic → its value → rejection region → conclusion
wrong: Conclusion → H0 and H1 → value → rejection region → statistic
Value → H0 and H1 → conclusion → rejection region → statistic
Rejection region → value → H0 and H1 → statistic → conclusion
questions.e: The seminar file always uses the same five steps in this order.

questions.q: The value of the test statistic is not in the rejection region. How does the seminar file word the conclusion?
questions.answer: The value of the test statistic is not inconsistent with H0
wrong: The value of the test statistic is inconsistent with H0
questions.e: The file never says H0 is true; it says the result is not inconsistent with H0.

questions.q: A company worries the mean number of passengers has dropped below 36. Which H1?
questions.e: A worry about a decline means a left-tailed alternative.

questions.q: H1: E(X) ≠ 28,306 at α = 0.06. Which quantile is the critical value?
Normal population, σ² unknown, n = 15. Which distribution does the test statistic have if H0 is true?
questions.e: Normal population and unknown variance → T ~ t(n − 1) = t(14).

questions.q: In the z-test of a proportion, what goes under the square root?
questions.answer: π0(1 − π0)/n, using the value from H0
wrong: p(1 − p)/n, using the sample proportion
questions.e: In the test we assume H0 is true, so π0 is used.

questions.q: The same difference between p and π0 is not significant for n = 250 but is significant for n = 1,500. Why?
questions.answer: A bigger sample makes the standard error smaller, so |z| grows
wrong: A bigger sample always rejects H0
questions.e: z = (p − π0)/√(π0(1 − π0)/n): with larger n the denominator shrinks, so |z| gets bigger.

questions.q: A goodness-of-fit test has 6 categories. How many degrees of freedom does the chi-square distribution have?
n = 200 and π0 = 0.25 for a category. What is its expected frequency n′?
Where is the rejection region of the chi-square goodness-of-fit test?
questions.answer: Always in the right tail: g ≥ χ²(1−α)
questions.e: Large g means a big difference between observed and expected, so only the right tail.

questions.q: General distribution in the population, n = 50 (large enough). Which test of the mean?
questions.e: With a large random sample and a general distribution, Z ≈ N(0, 1).

questions.q: Left-tailed z-test, α = 0.01, z = −2.687. What is the conclusion?
questions.answer: Inconsistent with H0 in favour of H1 (z ≤ −2.326)
Only that H0 was rejected; nothing about practical importance
wrong: That the difference is large and important
That the sample is not random
questions.e: The seminar file stresses it is just a label, not practical significance.

questions.q: Why is a test at an 80 % significance level useless in practice?
questions.answer: The rejection region is huge, so the type 1 error probability is huge
wrong: It needs a sample of 80 elements
The test statistic cannot be calculated
questions.e: The file’s note: critical values are very close to zero, so almost any value falls into W.

vocab.meaning: A procedure that uses a random sample to judge a hypothesis about a population parameter or distribution.
H0: the parameter equals the claimed value (contains the equality).
H1: what the research expects, with >, < or ≠ (or non H0).
The claim the researcher wants to support, decided before any calculation; it guides the choice of H1.
α: the accepted probability of rejecting H0 although it is true.
Rejecting H0 although H0 is true; its probability is α.
A random variable (T, Z, G) whose distribution is known if H0 is true.
The number (t, z, g) calculated from the sample.
W(α): values of the test statistic that are inconsistent with H0; bounded by quantiles from the tables.
The quantile that forms the boundary of the rejection region, e.g. z(1−α/2).
H1 with >: rejection region in the right tail.
H1 with ≠: rejection region in both tails, each with α/2.
Mean of a normal population with unknown variance: t = (x̄ − μ0)/s · √n, T ~ t(n − 1).
z = (p − π0)/√(π0(1 − π0)/n), approximately N(0, 1) for a large sample.
Chi-square test of whether the distribution in the population matches assumed proportions π0,j; df = k − 1.
n′ = n · π0,j: the count expected in category j if H0 is true.

facts: The null hypothesis always contains the {equality|inequality|sample mean|significance level}.
The significance level is the probability of a type {1|2|3|0} error.
Every hypothesis test in 4ST601 follows {5|3|4|6} steps.
If the value is outside the rejection region, it is not {inconsistent|consistent|significant|equal} with H0.
A worry about a decline gives a {left|right|two|both}-tailed test.
A test of whether a value is the same gives a {two|left|right|one}-tailed test.
A normal population with unknown variance uses the {t|z|chi-square|F} distribution.
The denominator of the z-test of a proportion uses the value of pi from {H0|the sample|H1|the table}.
The goodness-of-fit test with k categories has k minus {1|2|0|k} degrees of freedom.
The rejection region of the goodness-of-fit test is always in the {right|left|middle|both} tail.
